title: Explain Master-Slave architecture, its use cases, and what happens if the master or a slave dies.
shortTitle: Explain Master-Slave architecture, its use cases, and what happens if the master or a slave dies

s1_definition.profdef: Master-slave, also increasingly called primary-replica, is a replication architecture in which one node, the master, accepts all writes and is the authoritative source of truth, while one or more slave nodes receive a continuous copy of the master's data and typically serve read traffic. It is used to scale reads, provide high availability, and support backups and analytics without burdening the master. If a slave dies, reads simply shift to other slaves or the master with no data loss; if the master dies, writes stop until a slave is promoted to master, either manually or by automated failover, with a risk of losing writes that had not yet replicated.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India keeps one official master ledger that only the head cashier can write to, so there is one authoritative record of every transaction. Several assistants keep up-to-date photocopies of that ledger, and when customers like Rajesh just want to read their balance, they ask an assistant, which keeps the head cashier free to record new transactions. If one assistant is off sick, customers just ask another, no harm done. But if the head cashier suddenly leaves, nobody can record new transactions until one assistant is officially promoted to head cashier, and any entry the cashier had written but not yet shared with the assistants could be lost.
s1_definition.oneliner: One master takes all writes as the source of truth and replicates to slaves that serve reads; a dead slave just loses some read capacity, but a dead master halts writes until a slave is promoted, risking the loss of not-yet-replicated writes.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Master-slave, also increasingly called primary-replica, is a replication architecture in which one node, the master, accepts all writes and is the authoritative source of truth, while one or more slave nodes receive a continuous copy of the master's data and typically serve read traffic. It is used to scale reads, provide high availability, and support backups and analytics without burdening the master. If a slave dies, reads simply shift to other slaves or the master with no data loss; if the master dies, writes stop until a slave is promoted to master, either manually or by automated failover, with a risk of losing writes that had not yet replicated.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India keeps one official master ledger that only the head cashier can write to, so there is one authoritative record of every transaction. Several assistants keep up-to-date photocopies of that ledger, and when customers like Rajesh just want to read their balance, they ask an assistant, which keeps the head cashier free to record new transactions. If one assistant is off sick, customers just ask another, no harm done. But if the head cashier suddenly leaves, nobody can record new transactions until one assistant is officially promoted to head cashier, and any entry the cashier had written but not yet shared with the assistants could be lost.

**One line to remember:** One master takes all writes as the source of truth and replicates to slaves that serve reads; a dead slave just loses some read capacity, but a dead master halts writes until a slave is promoted, risking the loss of not-yet-replicated writes.

sections.s2_technical:
The core idea is a single authoritative writer and multiple read copies. All write operations, inserts, updates, and deletes, go to the master, which applies them and records them in a replication log. Each slave connects to the master and continuously receives that stream of changes, applying them in order so its data converges to match the master's. Reads can be served by slaves, which spreads read load across many machines, while the master is freed to concentrate on writes. This asymmetry, one writer and many readers, is what makes the pattern useful and also what shapes its failure behaviour.

Replication can be asynchronous or synchronous, and this choice is central to understanding failures. In asynchronous replication, the master commits a write and acknowledges the client immediately, then ships the change to slaves afterwards; this is fast and is the common default, but it means a slave can lag slightly behind, and if the master dies before a recently committed write reaches any slave, that write is lost. In synchronous replication, the master waits for at least one slave to confirm it has received the write before acknowledging the client; this prevents that specific data loss but adds latency to every write and can stall if a slave is slow, so many systems use a middle ground like semi-synchronous replication where the master waits for just one slave.

A consequence of serving reads from slaves is replication lag, which creates eventual consistency on the read path. A client that writes to the master and immediately reads from a slave might not see its own write yet, because the change has not replicated. In banking this matters: showing Rajesh a stale balance right after his transfer would be confusing or wrong. The mitigations are to route reads that must be fresh, like read-your-own-writes, to the master, to use a short window where recent writers read from the master, or to track replication position and only serve reads from sufficiently caught-up slaves.

The use cases follow directly. Read scaling is the biggest: read-heavy workloads, like dashboards, reporting, and balance lookups, are offloaded to slaves so the master is not overwhelmed. High availability: because slaves hold full copies, the system can survive a node loss and, with failover, keep running. Backups and heavy analytics: you can take backups or run expensive reporting queries against a slave without slowing the master that serves live transactions. Geographic read locality: placing slaves near users reduces read latency.

Now the failure scenarios in detail. If a slave dies, the impact is limited and graceful: that slave's share of read traffic is redistributed to the remaining slaves or temporarily to the master, there is no data loss because the master still holds everything, and once the slave is repaired it reconnects and catches up from the replication log. Writes are entirely unaffected because the master is untouched. This is the easy case.

If the master dies, it is serious because the system loses its only writer. All writes stop immediately, and reads from slaves may continue but will become increasingly stale. Recovery means promoting one slave to become the new master, which can be manual or handled by an automated failover controller that detects the master is down, selects the most up-to-date slave, promotes it, and repoints the other slaves and the application at it. The key risks are data loss, since any write that the old master committed but had not yet replicated under asynchronous replication is gone, and split-brain, where a network partition makes two nodes each believe they are master and accept conflicting writes, which is why robust failover uses quorum and fencing to ensure only one master exists. After promotion the old master, when it recovers, must rejoin as a slave of the new master rather than resuming as master.

Senior nuances: master-slave scales reads but not writes, since all writes still funnel through one master, so write-heavy systems need sharding or multi-master designs instead; automated failover must guard against split-brain with fencing and quorum; monitor replication lag as a first-class metric; and for strict banking correctness prefer at least semi-synchronous replication on critical data so an acknowledged write is guaranteed to survive a master failure.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's database was overwhelmed because every balance lookup, statement view, and report hit the same node that also processed transfers. This is exactly the read-scaling use case, where reads move to slaves so the master handles only writes.

Problem 2 — One read replica crashed during peak hours. This is exactly the slave-death case, where read traffic simply shifts to the remaining replicas with no data loss and writes continue unaffected.

Problem 3 — The master node failed one night, and writes stopped entirely. This is exactly the master-death case, requiring promotion of a slave to master, with careful attention to any writes that had not yet replicated.

Our mini-project simulates the architecture. The code defines a `Master` that accepts writes and keeps a replication log, `Slave` nodes that pull and apply the log and serve reads, a `Cluster` that routes writes to the master and reads to slaves, and a demo that performs transfers on the master, reads balances from slaves, kills a slave to show graceful read redistribution, and kills the master to show promotion of a slave, including a write that was not yet replicated to illustrate the data-loss risk.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d target/classes src/main/java/com/bank/masterslave/MasterSlaveDemo.java

# Run
java -cp target/classes com.bank.masterslave.MasterSlaveDemo

# Expected: writes on master replicate to slaves; killing a slave keeps reads+writes working;
# killing the master halts writes and promotes a slave, losing the unreplicated write (async).
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's account SAV2001 starting at 1,000,000 rupees, with a series of balance updates and two node failures.

Step 1: The cluster writes the initial balance to the master, which records it in its replication log, and then replicates it to the slaves so each slave holds a copy. A read from a slave now returns the correct balance, which is the normal read-scaling path with writes on the master and reads on the slaves.

Step 2: A transfer reduces the balance, the write goes to the master, and replication copies it to the slaves, so a read from a slave reflects the new balance. The master handled the write and the slaves handled the read, keeping the two kinds of load separate.

Step 3: One slave dies. The impact is graceful: reads simply go to the surviving slave, writes continue on the master unaffected, and no data is lost because the master still holds everything. A subsequent write and read both succeed, demonstrating that a slave failure only reduces read capacity.

Step 4: A new write sets the balance but, to illustrate the risk, the master dies before that write is replicated to any slave. Because the write never left the master under asynchronous replication, the slaves do not have it.

Step 5: With the master dead, writes halt entirely, and the cluster promotes the most caught-up surviving slave to be the new master. Because that slave never received the last write, the promoted master's balance reflects the previous value, so the unreplicated write is lost. The output shows normal operation, the graceful slave failure, and the master failover with the lost write, which is exactly why critical banking data uses at least semi-synchronous replication.

```
2026-10-24 15:14:22 INFO    read from slave: SAV2001 balance = 950000
2026-10-24 15:14:22 WARNING slave-1 died → reads shift to remaining replicas (writes unaffected)
2026-10-24 15:14:22 INFO    read still works from surviving slave: 900000
2026-10-24 15:14:22 WARNING master died BEFORE replicating last write (Rs.880000)
2026-10-24 15:14:22 INFO    promoted most-caught-up slave to new master (fencing prevents split-brain)
2026-10-24 15:14:22 SEVERE  after promotion, new master balance = 900000 (the unreplicated Rs.880000 write was LOST under async replication)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  WRITES                          READS
    │ (inserts/updates)            │ (balance, statements, reports)
    ▼                              ▼
  ┌──────────┐  replication log  ┌──────────┐  ┌──────────┐
  │ MASTER    │─────────────────▶│ Slave 1   │  │ Slave 2   │
  │ (sole     │─────────────────▶│ (replica) │  │ (replica) │
  │  writer)  │                   └──────────┘  └──────────┘
  └──────────┘                        ▲              ▲
                                       └──── reads ───┘

  ── Slave dies ──
  Slave 1 ✗ → reads go to Slave 2 / master ; writes unaffected ; NO data loss

  ── Master dies ──
  MASTER ✗ → all writes HALT
     │ failover controller: pick most caught-up slave
     ▼
  Slave 2 ──promote──▶ NEW MASTER (fencing prevents split-brain)
     │ unreplicated writes on old master = LOST (async)
     ▼
  old master recovers → rejoins as a SLAVE of the new master
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Master-Slave Replication (FAANG Level) ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Primary-Replica: one writer, many read copies                │
  │   WHY: scale reads + availability without multi-writer cost  │
  │ Leader Election / Failover: promote a replica on master loss │
  │   WHY: restore write capability automatically                │
  │ Fencing: ensure exactly one active master                    │
  │   WHY: prevent split-brain conflicting writes                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: Master writes+logs; Slave applies+reads; Cluster routes    │
  │ O: add a replica = new Slave, routing unchanged               │
  │ L: any promoted slave behaves as a master                     │
  │ D: app depends on Cluster routing, not a specific node        │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ─────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌──────────┐ replicates ┌──────────┐   routed by  ┌──────────┐
  │ Master    │───────────▶│ Slave    │◀─────────────│ Cluster   │
  │ data,log  │            │ data,    │  write→master │ +write    │
  │ +write    │            │ appliedUp│  read→slave   │ +read     │
  └──────────┘            └──────────┘               │ +promote  │
                                                     └──────────┘

  ── State: node roles on master failure ───────────────────────
  [MASTER alive] ──dies──▶ [NO MASTER, writes halt]
        │                         │ failover
        ▼                         ▼
  [SLAVE] ───promote───▶ [NEW MASTER]  (old master rejoins as SLAVE)

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1. write(SAV2001) → master only → append replication log
  2. replicate() → each live slave applies log
  3. readFromSlave() → served by a caught-up slave
  4. killMaster() → writes halt
  5. promoteSlaveToMaster() → pick max(appliedUpTo), fence others
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Master-slave, which many systems now call primary-replica, is a replication architecture with a single authoritative writer and multiple read copies. All writes go to the master, which applies them and records them in a replication log, and each slave continuously receives that stream of changes and applies them in order so its data converges to the master's. Reads are served from the slaves, which spreads read load across many machines and frees the master to concentrate on writes. That asymmetry of one writer and many readers is what makes the pattern useful and also what shapes its failure behaviour.

A key decision is asynchronous versus synchronous replication. With asynchronous replication the master commits and acknowledges the client immediately, then ships the change to slaves afterwards, which is fast but means a slave can lag and a write committed just before a master crash can be lost. With synchronous replication the master waits for a slave to confirm before acknowledging, which prevents that loss but adds latency, so many systems use semi-synchronous replication where the master waits for just one slave. Serving reads from slaves also introduces replication lag and eventual consistency on the read path, so a client that writes and immediately reads a slave might not see its own write, which in banking I handle by routing reads that must be fresh to the master.

The use cases follow directly. The biggest is read scaling, offloading read-heavy work like balance lookups, dashboards, and reports to slaves. Then high availability, because slaves hold full copies so the system can survive a node loss with failover. Then backups and heavy analytics run against a slave so they do not slow the master, and geographic read locality by placing slaves near users. The important limitation is that master-slave scales reads but not writes, since every write still funnels through one master, so a write-heavy system needs sharding or multi-master instead.

On the failure questions: if a slave dies, the impact is graceful, its read traffic shifts to the other slaves or the master, there is no data loss because the master still holds everything, writes are unaffected, and the repaired slave reconnects and catches up from the log. If the master dies, it is serious because the system loses its only writer, so all writes stop immediately and slave reads grow stale. Recovery means promoting the most up-to-date slave to be the new master, manually or by an automated failover controller, and the two big risks are data loss, since any write the old master had not yet replicated under async replication is gone, and split-brain, where a partition makes two nodes each think they are master, which robust failover prevents with quorum and fencing; the old master, when it recovers, must rejoin as a slave. On my project at National Bank of India we moved all reads to replicas to relieve an overloaded database, survived a replica crash with no impact, and when the master failed we promoted a replica, which is exactly why we used semi-synchronous replication on critical data so an acknowledged write was guaranteed to survive a master failure. I also always monitor replication lag as a first-class metric.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that one master takes all writes as the source of truth and replicates to slaves that serve reads, so it scales reads, availability, and backups but not writes; a dead slave only loses read capacity with no data loss, while a dead master halts writes until a slave is promoted, risking the loss of not-yet-replicated writes and requiring fencing to avoid split-brain.
